newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu vows to remain in power in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu vows to remain in power in Israel.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected calls to resign and vowed to lead Israel into the 21st century as prosecutors weighed whether to indict him in a corruption scandal.

"This government is not going anywhere. We are not going anywhere. We are staying where the people and history have put us," Netanyahu told cheering supporters at the headquarters of his Likukd party in Tel Aviv on Thursday.
"I have come to tell you today that we will continue to lead the state of Israel...We will continue on this path until the year 2000 and I tell you, beyond the year 2000."

Dropping a political bombshell, police on Wednesday wrapped up a three-month probe into the short-lived appointment of an attorney general by recommending Netanyahu be indicted on charges of fraud and breach of trust.

Prosecutors pored over the 995-page police report at a secluded location near Jerusalem, keeping Netanyahu's political life in limbo as they considered whether he would become the first Israeli prime minister to face criminal charges.
"We are trying to finish up and hope to do so before the holiday," State Attorney Edna Arbel said on Thursday, referring to the Passover festival of freedom starting on Monday.

The question mark over Netanyahu's future overshadowed a peace mission by U.S. presidential envoy Dennis Ross, who met in Gaza with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat late on Thursday. No details of their talks were immediately available.

In Washington, the White House vowed to press ahead with its peace efforts despite the political crisis in Israel. It said it was up to the Israelis to resolve what it called a "domestic legal matter".
Israel's main opposition Labour party demanded Netanyahu resign.

"I think the prime minister should reach the proper conclusion and any attempt to delay this will not help anyone," former Labour prime minister Shimon Peres, who lost last May's election to the right-wing Netanyahu, told reporters.
But prosecutors could still ignore the police recommendations to charge Netanyahu over the appointment of Likud activist Roni Bar-On as attorney general three months ago.
Israel's Channel One has been alleging ever since that a Netanyahu ally on trial for corruption, politician Aryeh Deri, pushed Bar-On for the job in the hope of winning a plea bargain.

The television said Deri had promised that in return, his Shas party would support Netanyahu's deal with the Palestinians to redeploy in the West Bank town of Hebron. Netanyahu has called the allegations "nonsense".
In a show of bravado in front of Likud party faithful -- who hailed him with shouts of "Bibi, king of Israel" -- Netanyahu told Labour it would not dethrone him.

"To all those eager to replace us: I can say that every two weeks they take their suits out of the closet to air in the sun -- put them back, put them back," Netanyahu said, his voice dripping with disdain.
Netanyahu, 47, is under no formal legal obligation to quit if indicted, although several jurists said they expected he would step down to conform with what one called "public norms".
Under Israeli law, the resignation of a prime minister automatically brings down the government and a general election is held within 60 days.
Netanyahu's ruling coalition of mainly right-wing and religious parties could crumble from within if he is charged and decides to remain in office.

Trade and Industry Minister Natan Sharansky, leader of the Yisrael ba-Aliya party which holds seven of the 66 seats the coalition controls in the 120-member parliament, has said the government could not survive even if "only 10 percent" of the allegations proved true.
Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani's Third Way party, with four seats, is also widely expected to bolt the coalition if Netanyahu refuses to quit after an indictment.
Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh railed in an Israel Radio interview on Thursday against what he said were politicians "ganging up" on Netanyahu.

Naveh said the course of history would be changed if the Israeli leader -- whose decision to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem plunged the Israel-PLO peace process into crisis -- quit after an indictment.
"But there would be no way to turn back the clock after he is acquitted," Naveh said.
